tracks.name: MongoDB Basics
tracks.description: Documents, collections, and the shell commands that create and read data.

lessons.title: 1. Documents and collections
lessons.summary: MongoDB stores JSON-like documents in collections — not rows in tables.

activities.title: A collection of documents
activities.instruction: A MongoDB database holds collections, and a collection holds documents. A document is a JSON-like object — a set of fields with values. Documents in one collection don't need the same shape.

activities.title: What is a document?
activities.question: In MongoDB, what is a document closest to?
choices: A JSON-like object with fields and values
activities.answer: A JSON-like object with fields and values
activities.explanation: A document is a JSON-like object. It lives in a collection the way a row lives in a table, but it carries its own field names and can differ from its neighbours.

activities.title: Insert a document
activities.instruction: Insert a document into the `books` collection with the title 'Dune' and 412 pages.

teaching.text: MongoDB is a **document database**. Instead of tables and rows it stores **documents** — JSON-like objects — inside **collections**.

Every document gets a unique `_id` automatically if you don't supply one. Documents in the same collection are allowed to have different fields — one product can have `wireless`, another can leave it out.
These lessons use the MongoDB Shell (`mongosh`). `use('shop')` switches to the `shop` database and creates it on the first write.

lessons.task: Insert a document into the `books` collection with the title 'Dune' and 412 pages.
lessons.starterCode:
use('library');

// Insert one document into the books collection
hints: `db.books.insertOne({ ... })` inserts one document.
db.books.insertOne({ title: 'Dune', pages: 412 });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why might it be useful that documents in one collection don't all share the same fields?

lessons.title: 2. Inserting documents
lessons.summary: Add one document, or many at once.

activities.title: One or many
activities.instruction: `insertOne()` adds a single document. `insertMany()` takes an **array** of documents and adds them all in one round trip to the server.

activities.title: The insertMany() argument
activities.question: What does `insertMany()` take as its argument?
activities.explanation: insertMany() expects an array, even when it only holds one document.

activities.title: Add two products
activities.instruction: Use `insertMany()` to add two products: Mouse at 19 and Monitor at 199.

teaching.text: `db.<collection>.insertOne(document)` writes one document. `db.<collection>.insertMany(arrayOfDocuments)` writes several.
Both return a result object with `acknowledged` and the `insertedIds` the server assigned. If the collection doesn't exist yet, MongoDB creates it on the first insert.
A write is atomic **per document**, not per batch — if one document in an `insertMany()` fails, the others already written stay written unless you use a transaction.

lessons.task: Use insertMany() to add two products: Mouse at 19 and Monitor at 199.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Add both products in a single call
hints: `insertMany()` takes an array, so open with `[` and close with `]`.
db.products.insertMany([{ name: 'Mouse', price: 19 }, { name: 'Monitor', price: 199 }]);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you prefer insertMany() over calling insertOne() twice?

lessons.title: 3. Reading documents
lessons.summary: Read documents back out of a collection.

activities.title: find and findOne
activities.instruction: `find()` returns every matching document as a cursor. `findOne()` returns just the first match, or `null` when nothing matches.

activities.title: find() with no filter
activities.question: What does `find()` with no arguments return?
choices: An error — a filter is required
activities.explanation: With no filter, every document matches. findOne() with no filter returns just the first one.

activities.title: Read the Monitor document
activities.instruction: Use `findOne()` to read the product whose name is 'Monitor'.

teaching.text: Reading data works the same way for one document or many: pass a filter object describing which documents you want.
`{}` matches every document. `find()` gives you a **cursor** — a lazy pointer you can sort, limit, or iterate instead of loading everything into memory at once.
An empty result from `findOne()` is `null`, not an error. Always check before reading fields off it.

lessons.task: Use findOne() to read the product named 'Monitor'.
hints: `db.products.findOne({ ... })` returns the first document that matches.
db.products.findOne({ name: 'Monitor' });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does find() hand back a cursor instead of an array of every document?

lessons.title: 4. Projections
lessons.summary: Return only the fields you actually need.

activities.title: Pick the fields
activities.instruction: The second argument to `find()` is a **projection**: list the fields you want with `1`, or the fields you don't want with `0`. You can't mix the two styles, except for `_id`.

activities.title: Reading a projection
activities.question: What does the projection `{ name: 1, _id: 0 }` do?
choices: Returns only the name field, without _id
activities.answer: Returns only the name field, without _id
activities.explanation: 1 means include, 0 means exclude. _id is included by default, so you switch it off explicitly.

activities.title: Project name and price
activities.instruction: Find every product but return only the `name` and `price` fields, hiding `_id`.

teaching.text: Documents can be large. A projection trims the shape of each result so you only transfer the fields you use.
`1` includes a field, `0` excludes it. Mixing include and exclude in the same projection is an error — the one exception is `_id`, which you can always turn off.
Projections also help queries use a **covered index**: if every field you ask for lives in an index, MongoDB never has to read the full document.

lessons.task: Find every product, returning only name and price and hiding _id.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Every product, but only the name and price fields
hints: The projection is the second argument to `find()`.
db.products.find({}, { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What do you gain by projecting away fields you don't display?

tracks.name: Queries & Updates
tracks.description: Filter, update, and delete documents with MongoDB's query operators.

lessons.title: 5. Comparison operators
lessons.summary: Match documents by comparing field values.

activities.title: Greater and less than
activities.instruction: Operators start with `$` and sit inside the field they test: `{ price: { $gt: 20 } }` means 'price greater than 20'. You can combine two bounds on one field.

activities.title: Cheaper than 20
activities.question: Which query finds products cheaper than 20?
activities.explanation: $lt means less than, $gt means greater than, and { price: 20 } means exactly 20.

activities.title: Products at 100 or more
activities.instruction: Find every product whose price is 100 or more.

teaching.text: A filter object answers 'which documents?'. Equality is the default — `{ name: 'Mouse' }` — and comparisons use `$` operators.
`$gt` and `$lt` are strict; `$gte` and `$lte` include the boundary. Several operators on one field are combined with AND.
`$ne` (not equal) also matches documents that don't have the field at all — worth remembering when data is uneven.

lessons.task: Find every product whose price is 100 or more.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Products that cost 100 or more
hints: Use `$gte` so the price 100 itself is included.
db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 100 } });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does MongoDB need `$gt` instead of letting you write `price > 20`?

lessons.title: 6. Lists and patterns
lessons.summary: Match any value in a list, or text against a pattern.

activities.title: $in and $regex
activities.instruction: `$in` matches any value in an array. `$regex` matches a field against a regular expression, and `$options: 'i'` makes it case-insensitive.

activities.title: What $in matches
activities.question: What does `{ name: { $in: ['Mouse', 'Monitor'] } }` match?
choices: Documents whose name is either Mouse or Monitor
Documents whose name contains the word Mouse or Monitor
Documents with both a Mouse and a Monitor field
activities.answer: Documents whose name is either Mouse or Monitor
activities.explanation: $in compares the whole field value against the list — it is an exact match against any one entry, not a substring search.

activities.title: Names starting with M
activities.instruction: Find every product whose name starts with 'M', using `$regex`.

teaching.text: `$in` is the compact form of several equality checks. `$regex` handles text that follows a pattern.
In a regex, `^` anchors to the start of the string, so `'^M'` means 'begins with M'. Without an anchor the pattern matches anywhere in the value.
An unanchored `$regex` can't use an index efficiently — it has to scan the collection. Anchoring the pattern or using a text index keeps large collections fast.

lessons.task: Use $regex to find products whose name starts with M.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Products whose name starts with M
hints: `^` anchors the pattern to the start of the string.
db.products.find({ name: { $regex: '^M' } });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When is $in clearer than chaining several $or conditions?

lessons.title: 7. Updating documents
lessons.summary: Change fields on documents that already exist.

activities.title: Change a field
activities.instruction: `updateOne(filter, update)` changes the first matching document. Update operators like `$set` and `$inc` describe *what* to change — a plain object as the second argument replaces the whole document instead.

activities.title: No operator
activities.question: What happens if the second argument is `{ price: 45 }` with no `$set`?
choices: The price field is updated to 45
The whole document is replaced with `{ price: 45 }`
activities.answer: The whole document is replaced with `{ price: 45 }`
activities.explanation: Without update operators, the second argument is a replacement document — every other field disappears.

activities.title: Set the Mouse price
activities.instruction: Use `updateOne()` with `$set` to set the price of 'Mouse' to 25.

teaching.text: Writes that change existing data take a filter first, so the same query language you learned for `find()` selects *which* documents get updated.
`$set` changes the listed fields and leaves the rest alone. `$inc` adds to a number, `$unset` removes a field, and `updateMany()` applies the change to every match.
The result object reports `matchedCount` and `modifiedCount` — a filter that matched nothing is not an error, so check `matchedCount` when a change seems to vanish.

lessons.task: Use updateOne() with $set to set the Mouse price to 25.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Change the Mouse price to 25
hints: Pass the filter first, then the update: `{ $set: { ... } }`.
db.products.updateOne({ name: 'Mouse' }, { $set: { price: 25 } });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why are update operators like $set safer than passing a plain object?

lessons.title: 8. Counting and deleting
lessons.summary: Count what you have and remove documents you no longer need.

activities.title: Removing documents
activities.instruction: `countDocuments(filter)` counts matches. `deleteOne()` removes the first match and `deleteMany()` removes every match.

activities.title: One versus many
activities.question: What is the difference between `deleteOne()` and `deleteMany()`?
choices: deleteOne removes the first match; deleteMany removes every match
deleteOne removes a field; deleteMany removes a document
They are identical — only the name differs
activities.answer: deleteOne removes the first match; deleteMany removes every match
activities.explanation: The filter is the same; only how many matches get removed differs.

activities.title: Delete and count
activities.instruction: Delete every product priced below 20, then print how many products remain.

teaching.text: Counting and deleting reuse the filter object, which makes it easy to check what you are about to remove.
`deleteMany({})` with an empty filter clears the whole collection — the documents go, but the collection and its indexes remain.
Run the same filter through `find()` before you delete. `deletedCount` in the result tells you afterwards how many documents actually went.

lessons.task: Delete products under 20, then print how many products remain.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Delete cheap products, then count what's left
hints: Use `$lt: 20` as the filter for both the delete and the count.

db.products.deleteMany({ price: { $lt: 20 } });
console.log(db.products.countDocuments());
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should you run find() with the same filter before you call deleteMany()?

tracks.name: Aggregation & Node.js
tracks.description: Summarise data with pipelines and use MongoDB from a Node.js app.

lessons.title: 9. Sorting and paging
lessons.summary: Order results and page through them.

activities.title: Order and cap
activities.instruction: `sort()` takes fields with `1` for ascending or `-1` for descending. `limit()` caps how many documents come back, and `skip()` jumps ahead — together they page through results.

activities.title: Cheapest first
activities.question: Which sort puts the cheapest product first?
activities.explanation: 1 is ascending, so the smallest price comes first. -1 is descending, and limit() only caps the count.

activities.title: Two most expensive
activities.instruction: Find the two most expensive products.

teaching.text: Cursors are chainable. `find()` gives you the matches, then `sort()`, `skip()`, and `limit()` shape what you receive.
`1` sorts ascending and `-1` descending. Sorting happens on the server, before `limit()` trims the result — which is why `sort` + `limit` returns the top N, not a random N.
Sorting a field with no index forces an in-memory sort. Large collections need an index on the sort key to stay fast.

lessons.task: Find the two most expensive products.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// The two most expensive products
hints: Descending means `-1`, so the biggest price comes first.
db.products.find().sort({ price: -1 }).limit(2);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: How would skip() and limit() combine to show page 2 of a paginated list?

lessons.title: 10. Aggregation pipelines
lessons.summary: Transform documents in stages to build summaries.

activities.title: Stages in a pipeline
activities.instruction: `aggregate()` runs documents through a list of stages. Each stage takes the documents from the stage before it: `$match` filters, `$group` combines, and `$sum` adds up a field.

activities.title: What _id means in $group
activities.question: What does `_id` inside `$group` define?
choices: The unique id of the output document
The value documents are grouped by
The field to sort the output on
activities.answer: The value documents are grouped by
activities.explanation: In a $group stage, _id is the grouping key. `'$status'` means 'the status field of each document', while a literal string groups everything into one bucket.

activities.title: Count per status
activities.instruction: Group the orders by `status` and count how many orders are in each group.

teaching.text: Aggregation is how you compute things MongoDB can't express with a simple filter — totals, averages, counts per category.
A `$` in front of a value means 'read this field from the document', so `'$status'` is the value of status. `$sum: 1` counts documents because 1 is added for each one.
Put `$match` first in a pipeline. Stages run in order, so filtering early means every later stage works on fewer documents.

lessons.task: In the orders collection, group by status and count each group.
lessons.starterCode:
use('shop');

// Count the orders in each status
hints: The pipeline is an array, so each stage is its own object.
db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: '$status', count: { $sum: 1 } } }]);
lessons.reflectionPrompt: How is an aggregation pipeline different from chaining several find() queries together?

lessons.title: 11. Connecting from Node.js
lessons.summary: Reach MongoDB from your app with the official driver.

activities.title: One client per app
activities.instruction: `MongoClient` is the entry point. Create it once, call `connect()` (queries also connect lazily), pick a database with `db()`, and close the client when the app shuts down.

activities.title: What db() gives you
activities.question: What does `client.db('shop')` return?
choices: A database handle you can query collections from
activities.answer: A database handle you can query collections from
activities.explanation: db() returns a handle. `db.collection('products')` narrows it to one collection, and that's what you run queries against.

activities.title: Connect and count
activities.instruction: Create a `MongoClient` for `mongodb://localhost:27017`, connect, log the number of documents in the products collection, then close the client.

teaching.text: In your own code you don't type queries into a shell — you use a driver. Install it with `npm install mongodb` and import `MongoClient`.
The driver is asynchronous, so every query returns a promise — `await` the reads and writes. The object you build up (`client` → `db` → `collection`) mirrors the server's structure.
Keep one shared `MongoClient` for the whole process. Creating a client per request opens a new connection pool each time and exhausts the server's connection limit.

lessons.task: Connect to MongoDB from Node.js and log the number of products.
lessons.starterCode:
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';

// Connect, count the products, then close the client
hints: `new MongoClient(url)` creates the client; `await client.connect()` opens the pool.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is one shared MongoClient better than opening a connection per request?

lessons.title: 12. CRUD with the driver
lessons.summary: Insert, read, and update documents from your Node.js code.

activities.title: Same queries, different place
activities.instruction: A collection handle supports the same operations as the shell, as promises. `find()` returns a cursor, so call `toArray()` when you want the documents.

activities.title: What find() returns
activities.question: What does `find()` return from the Node.js driver?
choices: A cursor you convert with toArray()
A promise for exactly one document
activities.answer: A cursor you convert with toArray()
activities.explanation: find() returns a cursor so large result sets aren't loaded at once. toArray(), or a for-await loop, pulls the documents out.

activities.title: Insert then read
activities.instruction: Insert a product named 'Webcam' priced 35, then read every product under 50 into an array.

teaching.text: The driver API is the shell API with promises: `collection.insertOne()`, `find()`, `updateOne()`, `deleteOne()`. Filters and operators are identical.
`find()` returns a cursor, not an array — `await products.find()` alone hands back the cursor object. Add `.toArray()` for all documents, or `.next()` for one at a time.
Writes resolve with a result object (`insertedId`, `modifiedCount`, `deletedCount`), not the document itself. Read the field you need from the result.

lessons.task: Insert one product and read the products under 50 into an array.
lessons.starterCode:
const products = client.db('shop').collection('products');

// Insert a Webcam at 35, then read everything under 50
hints: `await products.insertOne({ ... })` then `await products.find({ price: { $lt: 50 } }).toArray()`.

await products.insertOne({ name: 'Webcam', price: 35 });
const cheap = await products.find({ price: { $lt: 50 } }).toArray();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you reach for findOne() instead of find().toArray() in an API route?
